justification: A pairs bold numbered sans headings with a readable serif body, giving clear section hierarchy. B's light-weight headings rely on rules for separation, so they read as weaker. B's body text is also light, and it hyphenates the link ("dash-board"), which slightly hurts readability. The layout and banner are otherwise nearly identical.

A's alignment is inconsistent. The Overview heading sits outdented at the far left while the body is indented. The Arabic heading and its rule overshoot past the right margin of the content column. B keeps every element on one consistent column with aligned rules and table, so it is calmer and cleaner. A's bolder heading gives slightly stronger hierarchy, but its misalignment outweighs that.

The tables are essentially identical in both designs. B shares one left edge for its headings, intro text and table, adds numbered section headings, and puts a running header and footer on its continuation page. A indents its body and table relative to the headings and offsets its title in the band, which reads slightly less aligned. Its section rules add little.

B uses bold sans numbered headings that stand out clearly against the serif body, and it treats References consistently as a section. A's light serif headings are weak, its rules after every short paragraph fragment the page, and its References heading is styled inconsistently. B's body text is slightly larger and more legible.

A's bold section heads (Income Statement, Balance Sheet) stand out clearly against the body text. B's light-weight heads are barely heavier than the captions, which weakens hierarchy. A's serif table text is a bit more legible. B's running header band and page footer are a nice touch. Both continue the table well with a repeated header row.

A keeps every element on one consistent column: the header title, rules, both language sections and the table share the same left and right edges. B's alignment is broken. The Overview heading hangs left of the body text, the Arabic rule and heading run past the right margin, and the rules are offset from each other. This gives B a ragged, disordered look. B's bold sans headings add contrast but clash with the serif body. A's restrained serif system reads as more coherent.

A pairs a confident blue title band with a sans heading and serif body, and uses rules to give each section a clear, regular rhythm. Its indented body text is readable, though References is oddly demoted under Discussion. B is a plain default Times layout with numbered headings. It is clean and consistent but visually flat and less refined.

A has inconsistent left edges: the Overview heading hangs at one margin, its body text is indented, and the Arabic heading overruns past the right rule. B keeps every element on a single consistent margin, and its Arabic text in the table is more legible. A's bolder Overview heading gives slightly stronger hierarchy, but B's alignment and coherence win.

The two designs share the same layout, structure and spacing, and both leave much of the lower page empty. Design A pairs a sans-serif with a navy band. Design B pairs a serif with a green band. Both have clean heading rules and the same table treatment with bilingual columns, so neither has a meaningful advantage.

Both designs paginate the same long table identically and both repeat the header row on the continuation page. A uses a crisp sans with tabular figures that align cleanly in the numeric columns. A's running header band on page 2 carries the title and section, and its footer reads "Page 2 of 2". B's serif oldstyle numerals are less legible in a dense financial table. B's page-2 top bar is a bare stripe with no labels.

The two layouts are nearly identical. B uses a bolder Arabic typeface, so its headings carry more weight and its body text reads more clearly. A's lighter, thinner face weakens heading contrast. B's bullets are also proper round markers, where A's look like small dots or zeros. B's margins are slightly wider, though both pages leave a large empty lower half.

A pairs a refined serif with a dark title band and consistent rule lines that give each section an even rhythm. Its References heading is too small next to the other section heads, and the equation font clashes slightly. B is plain default Times with heavy bold heads and a tiny, cramped equation. Overall it looks less finished, though its hierarchy is clear.

The two layouts are nearly identical. A's naskh-style Arabic face reads more naturally and gives body text clearer letterforms. B's geometric kufi-like face makes the body text and numerals (١٨) slightly harder to read. The green and navy bands are comparable.

Design A has misaligned margins: the Overview heading sits at the far left while its body text is indented, the Arabic heading overflows past the right margin, and the rule lines start at inconsistent points. Design B keeps every element on a single consistent column. Its Arabic heading is aligned properly at the right edge, the numbered headings read clearly, and the table sits flush with the text.

B's navy title band and sans headings look polished, but it numbers Abstract and References as sections ("1 Abstract", "6 References"), breaking academic convention and the section hierarchy (B1). A is plainer but keeps Abstract and References unnumbered and sections 1–4 correctly ordered, giving a cleaner, more correct structure (A1). Spacing and body text are comparable in both.

A's headings hang left at the margin while the body is indented well inside, and the header title is offset from both. This makes the left edges ragged and the text column feel disconnected. B aligns its headings, body, rules and title on one consistent left edge, and its serif type is cohesive and calm. A's bold sans headings give a little more contrast, but B's alignment and unity read better overall.

The two designs share the same structure and pagination. A's bold numbered section headings ("1 Income Statement") stand out more clearly than B's light-weight headings, which are easy to miss. A's serif table figures read more firmly than B's thin sans numerals, which look faint in the dense table. B's dark header band on page 2 is a nice touch, but it does not offset A's stronger heading hierarchy.

The two pages share the same structure. A sets everything in a refined serif with slightly more generous section spacing, so it reads calmer and fills the page more evenly (A1). B uses a sans-serif with tighter spacing and hyphenates the link as "dash-board" across lines. That leaves a larger empty area at the bottom of the page (B1).

A's bold sans numbered headings stand out more clearly than B's light, unnumbered serif headings. B's rule-separated sections are tidy, but its headings are weak. A keeps a tighter, more consistent rhythm between the English and Arabic sections. The tables are essentially equivalent.

B keeps the title, rules, headings and body on one clean left edge with even section spacing. A hangs its headings and rules far left of both the indented body and the title, so the page feels off-axis. A's justified serif body text also opens up loose word gaps. A's bold headings give stronger hierarchy than B's light-weight headings, but B reads more cohesively overall.

The two layouts are nearly identical. B's serif type is larger with a taller x-height, so the body text and table cells read more easily than in A, where the small Garamond-style text feels faint. B also pairs Arabic type whose weight matches the Latin text, while A's Arabic sits visually heavier than the light Latin. Both leave the lower page empty.

The two designs are nearly identical in layout. A uses a more traditional Arabic typeface with clearer bullet markers (solid dots and dash), and its numbers read clearly. B's geometric face renders bullets as tiny dots that are hard to see and makes the numerals look faint, which weakens list legibility. A's headings also carry slightly more weight against the body text.

Both share the same dark header band and ruled section structure. B's serif face suits an academic paper. It gives more generous spacing between rules and text, and its bolded References heading separates the back matter more clearly. A sets everything in a tight, light sans with cramped section gaps, and its References heading is undifferentiated.

B's numbered, bolder section headings give a clearer hierarchy. Its bullets are proper round dots. A uses a lighter weight and odd small bullet glyphs. A's rules add some structure, but B reads cleaner.

A uses bold sans headings with numbering and a consistent treatment through to References, so the structure is clear and the rhythm steady. B's light serif headings with rules are elegant. However, they are weak relative to the body text. References switches to a small bold style, which breaks the pattern. B's body text is also slightly smaller and lighter, which hurts readability.

B's bold sans headings over an indented serif body give clearer section hierarchy than A's light headings, which sit close in weight to the body text. A is more uniformly aligned, with the title and body on one left margin. B's title, though, is offset from its hanging headings. Its body also sits inset to the right, leaving the page slightly unbalanced. Overall, B reads more distinctly.

The two designs share a near-identical structure. B's sans-serif body and table text is larger and more legible next to the Arabic script, and its bolder table header reads more clearly. A's small, light serif body text looks faint and is harder to read at this size.

A sets the Arabic in a clean, consistent font. Its text block keeps the percent sign. B's body text uses a smaller, weaker font. It drops the % character, leaving a gap after ١٨ that changes the meaning. B's rules divide the sections clearly, but its saturated blue band is harsher than A's muted navy.

A drops the percent sign in the summary line, leaving a visible gap after ١٨. Its body text is also indented away from the right edge of the headings, so the column edge is ragged. B renders ١٨٪ correctly and aligns the headings and body on one right margin. B's Arabic face is also cleaner and more legible.

The two designs are nearly identical in layout. B pairs bold sans headings with serif body text, giving clearer section hierarchy. A's light serif headings and rule lines are elegant but weaker. B's "2" numbering beside the Arabic heading is a little awkward. The tables are equivalent.

A has the cleaner hierarchy: its serif headings sit on a single left margin with the body text, while B's bold sans headings hang outdented from indented body text. A's column is also slightly narrow, and its light regular-weight headings are less distinct. B's bolder headings scan more easily, and its wider rules and band give the page a fuller, better-proportioned measure. The overall edge goes to B.

B's navy title band and evenly ruled sections give a consistent, deliberate structure and clean sans-serif text. A's bold serif headings are strong but its plain, unstyled layout looks default. B's light headings are somewhat weak, and its 'References' heading is undersized. The equation in A is cramped and small. Overall B reads as more polished.

Both designs carry the same navy title band and short RTL content. B adds thin rules above each section, which give a clearer structure and a steadier rhythm. A numbers its section headings, which helps hierarchy a little. B's bullets and dashes are small and faint, which costs it slightly. On balance, B's separators make the page feel more organized and polished.

B renders the percent sign correctly, whereas A drops it and leaves a gap. B also aligns its body text flush with the rule edge, while A indents the body text inconsistently relative to the headings. B's clearer sans Arabic face and larger title make the hierarchy crisper.

Both designs share the same structure, and both repeat the table header after the page break. B's bold numbered sans headings ("1 Income Statement", "2 Balance Sheet") stand out more clearly than A's light serif headings with rules. B's text face is sturdier and its running header and footer aid navigation. A's elegant serif looks refined but reads lighter at small sizes.

The two designs share the same layout. A renders the Arabic text more cleanly and legibly, and its percent sign displays correctly (١٨٪). In B the percent sign is missing and leaves a gap after ١٨. B's body text is also smaller and thinner, and its paragraph and list indentation is misaligned against the right margin.

Both designs show the same split table with a repeated header. A keeps the title, headings, body text and table on one consistent left edge, and its single serif family pairs well with the dark navy band. B hangs its headings out to the left of the indented body and table, which makes the column alignment look uneven. B's bright blue band and geometric sans headings also clash slightly with its serif body text. A is more cohesive overall, though the difference is modest.

A keeps a single consistent left edge for the title, headings and body, with a calm navy band and even section spacing. B hangs its headings out to the left of the title and body indents. Its rules end short of the band edge, and the extra rules plus justified body text add clutter and uneven word spacing. B's saturated blue band is louder. The hierarchy is comparable in both.

A pairs bold numbered sans headings with serif body text, so the section heads stand out clearly and the text is comfortable to read. B uses light-weight headings that read weaker and relies on rule lines for separation. Its thin body text is slightly harder to read. The tables and the header band are nearly the same in both.

B uses bold, numbered sans headings that stand clearly above serif body text, giving a strong and readable hierarchy. A sets light-weight headings that are barely distinct from the body, and its many blue rules fragment the short content. A's References heading is also smaller than its other headings, which is inconsistent. B's spacing feels cleaner and more even.

Both are single-page RTL reports with a coloured header band. A separates its sections with rule lines and gives them more generous spacing, so it reads more clearly and the content fills more of the page. B's numbered headings help a little, but its content is tighter and leaves a larger empty lower half.

Design B keeps headings, rules and body on one consistent left edge, which gives a cleaner column. Its serif headings pair with the serif body. Design A hangs its bold sans headings at a different indent from the body text and the title. That leaves misaligned edges, and the justified summary paragraph has loose spacing. A's headings are stronger, but B reads more coherently overall.

B renders the % sign in the summary sentence, while A appears to drop it, leaving a gap after ١٨. That error weighs heavily. B's dividers sit on the same margins as its text column, so the page feels more aligned. A's dividers run wider than its text. A's Naskh-style face is more refined, but B's clean sans reads well, and its dark band is sober.

The two designs are nearly identical in structure. In A, the serif face gives the table's numerals even weight and clear alignment. B uses a light sans whose thin digits, such as 1,111, read faintly and with uneven spacing. B does add a running header band on page 2, but that is a small gain. A's tables read slightly more cleanly.

A aligns all content to one consistent margin: the English and Arabic sections and the table share the same left and right edges, and both headings are numbered. B's alignment is erratic. The Overview heading hangs outside the left margin and the body is indented. The Arabic heading and its rule overshoot the right margin, and the Arabic table text is undersized. This makes B look broken and unbalanced.

A pairs a strong navy title band with a clean sans face, and its thin rules give an even, consistent section rhythm. B is a plain default serif layout. Its bold numbered headings do give clear hierarchy, but its small body text and widely spaced sections feel generic and less polished. A's headings are light and somewhat weak, yet its rules compensate for this.

Both designs share the same structure and table. A pairs a consistent sans family across Latin and Arabic text and separates the bilingual sections with thin rules. This gives the English and Arabic sections a clean, parallel rhythm. B mixes a serif body with sans headings, and its Arabic heading shows an awkward "2" numbering placed next to the Arabic text. B's headings are bolder, but A's overall consistency and section banding read more polished.

A keeps every element on one consistent column. B misaligns its elements: the Overview heading hangs left of the body text, and the rules run at different widths. The Arabic heading spills past the right margin, and the table's Arabic labels are cramped and small. A's English and Arabic sections mirror each other cleanly, and its table is evenly aligned.

Both share the same layout. A uses a consistent sans pairing that matches the Arabic sans text more evenly and keeps the small body and table text crisper. B's light serif body and table text looks small and faint next to its heavier Arabic text, so it reads less clearly.

Both share the same structure and table continuation. B's bold numbered section heads ("1 Income Statement", "2 Balance Sheet") stand out more clearly than A's light-weight heads with rules. B's serif body and table figures read more comfortably than A's thin light sans. A's dark header band on page 2 is heavier, but that is minor.

Both layouts are nearly identical. A's sturdier serif sets English body and table text at a larger, more legible weight, and its bold table header reads more clearly. B's light, small Garamond-style face makes the body and table rows faint and harder to read. B's Arabic is somewhat bolder, but overall A reads more evenly.

B aligns its headings and body on one consistent left margin and uses numbered sections, which gives a cleaner reading line. A pushes the headings out to the left of the body text. Its rules end short of the right edge, and its justified paragraph opens visible word gaps, so the column looks misaligned and the page feels unbalanced.

A uses bold numbered sans headings that stand out clearly from the body text, and its serif body text is more legible. B's light serif headings ('Overview') are weak and close to body size, and its Arabic heading has no number. B's thin body text and pale table text read less easily. B's rule dividers add some structure, but A's hierarchy is clearer overall.

A uses bold numbered sans headings over a serif body, giving clear section hierarchy. B's light-weight headings are barely heavier than its body text. Its repeated rules carry more of the structure than the type does. Its References heading also shrinks inconsistently to body size, and the thin grey body text is lighter to read.

The two designs share the same layout, structure, and table, differing only in palette and typeface. A pairs a green band with a serif; B pairs a navy band with a sans-serif. Both render the bilingual content cleanly and leave the same large empty space below the table, so neither is clearly better.

A pairs a sans-serif heading face with a serif body and adds a navy title band, so the hierarchy is clearer and the page more polished. B's all-Times setting with a plain centered title is serviceable but flat. B's unnumbered Abstract and References are slightly more conventional, though that does not offset A's stronger visual structure. Both have similar empty lower pages.

A uses a cleaner, more consistent Arabic font, and its text aligns with the rule margins. In B the percent sign is missing, leaving a gap after ١٨ in the summary. B's body text is also indented inconsistently relative to the headings and rules. B's bright blue band is louder but no better than A's navy band.

A uses one consistent serif and a single left margin, with a dark navy band that sits quietly above the content, so the page feels cohesive and calm. B's bold sans headings give stronger hierarchy. However, B hangs its headings far left of the body indent. Its rules end short of the right edge, the body text is justified with uneven spacing, and the saturated blue band is louder. Together these make B less balanced.

B's Arabic typeface renders more cleanly and evenly. Its numbered headings give a clearer hierarchy. In A, the percent sign looks missing or broken after ١٨, leaving a gap. A's thin rules divide the sections but add little. Both leave the lower page empty and use a similar header band.

A's serif face suits an academic paper. Its looser section spacing fills the page more evenly, leaving less dead space at the bottom than B. B's sans is clean, but its body text is small and grey. B also gives References a rule and plain-weight treatment equal to the main sections, which muddies the hierarchy. A's bold References label reads as a distinct back-matter heading.

Both designs repeat the table header across the page break and leave a similarly empty second page. A's bold, numbered sans headings ("1 Income Statement", "2 Balance Sheet") stand out clearly from the serif body text. A also has a running header and "Page 2 of 2" for navigation. B's light, unnumbered headings are barely larger than the body text, so section breaks are weaker. B's lighter serif table text is also slightly fainter to read.

B adds a dark title band and rule-separated sections that give the page structure and a steady rhythm. Its equation is more legible than A's tiny one. However, B drops the section numbering, uses light headings, and makes the References heading smaller than the other sections, which weakens consistency. A is plain and clear but visually flat.

A aligns headings, body text and tables on one consistent left margin, and its numbered headings plus running header aid navigation. B hangs headings outdented past the indented body and table, which gives a ragged left edge. B also adds rule lines above its headings that compete with the table rules. Its saturated blue band is less refined than A's navy.

B's bold, numbered sans-serif headings contrast clearly with the serif body text, so sections are easy to scan. Its slightly larger body text reads more comfortably. A's light serif headings and small, light body text give weaker hierarchy, though its rule lines add some structure. Both layouts leave a similar empty area at the bottom of the page.

B's thin rules above each section give clearer separation, a steadier vertical rhythm, and fill the page better, leaving less dead space at the bottom. A has numbered headings, which help hierarchy slightly, but its sections float loosely with a large empty lower half.

The two designs are nearly identical. A numbers its section headings, which marks the order more explicitly. B replaces the numbers with full-width rule lines above each section. These rules give B a clearer sectional rhythm and spread the content further down the page, which slightly improves balance and use of space. One small flaw in B is that its navy rules clash with the green header band.

The two designs share the same structure. A uses a clean, consistent Arabic sans with a clear heading scale, and its percentage renders correctly (١٨٪). B's naskh-style text is small and faint, the percent sign in the summary line is missing and leaves an odd gap, and the saturated blue band feels heavier than A's dark navy. B's headings also sit flush right while its body text is indented, which is less consistent.

A's EB Garamond-style serif is elegant, and its rules mark the section breaks neatly. But its body text is small and light, and the Latin "Overview" heading is thin and weak. B uses bold sans headings and larger, clearer body text, which gives stronger hierarchy and easier reading. The headings mix numbered bold Latin with Arabic, which is slightly inconsistent. The tables are comparable.

The two layouts are nearly identical. B sets the Arabic in a more traditional naskh-style face with proper Arabic-Indic numerals (١٨٪, ١, ٢), which reads more naturally. A uses a geometric Latin-paired Arabic font with Persian-style numerals that look slightly off. The band colours differ, but both work.

Design A's layout is misaligned. The Overview heading hangs left of the body text, the Arabic heading extends beyond the right margin past the rule, and the rules start at different x-positions. Its Arabic text is also small relative to the Latin text. Design B keeps every element on one consistent column with matched rules, and its Arabic text is legible and comparable in size to the Latin. A does have a stronger bold heading and slightly larger table text, but B's coherent alignment wins.

The two layouts are nearly identical. A's Arabic typeface is a bit heavier and more legible. Its bullets are clearer round dots, while B's are tiny and faint. A's headings stand out with more weight. B's lighter, thinner type reads less firmly, though its wider margins are comparable.

A keeps headings and body on a single left margin with numbered sections, which gives a clean, consistent reading line. B hangs its headings into the left margin while indenting the body text, and its rule lines run off-centre. That leaves the page feeling lopsided. B also shrinks References to a small subheading that reads as part of Discussion, which muddles the hierarchy. B's saturated blue band is louder, but A's navy header sits more calmly with the text.

A is a plain, consistent academic layout. Its numbered sections and References use the same heading level, and the margins are even. B has a striking blue title band, but the band is offset from the text column. Its body text is indented well past the headings, which wastes width. The rules between sections chop the page into pieces. References is demoted to a small subhead that reads as part of Discussion. Overall, B's polish comes with structural inconsistencies.

The two designs share a near-identical structure. B's Arabic typeface is more traditional and legible with clearer bullet glyphs. A's geometric font renders the bullets as tiny dots that read poorly. The green and navy bands are equivalent in effect.

The two designs share the same structure. B's serif typeface feels more refined. Its line spacing is more generous, and its content fills more of the page, which reduces the empty bottom area. A breaks the link across lines as "the dash-board", while B keeps "the dashboard" intact. A's light sans-serif headings are slightly weaker.

A keeps a consistent left edge: the title, rules, headings and table all share one margin. B hangs its headings out to the left of an indented table and body text, which breaks alignment. B's banner title is also centred while its headings are left-aligned. A adds a running header band on page 2 and pairs a light heading style with a clean sans table, which reads more cohesively. B's bolder headings are stronger, but the mixed alignment and serif table text feel less disciplined.

A separates its sections with rules, so the short content reads as a structured report and the page feels more anchored. B has numbered headings but no dividers. The numbering in B also clashes with the numbered recommendations list, and its content looks a little cramped against the header band. The two designs are close overall.

B pairs bold sans headings with a serif body, so the section heads stand out clearly. A's light-weight headings are close in tone to its body text, which weakens the hierarchy. B's indented body makes each section easier to scan. B's misaligned title and left-shifted heading column are small flaws but do not outweigh this.

Both designs split the same table across pages with repeated headers. A's bold sans section heads ('Income Statement', 'Balance Sheet') stand out clearly from the serif body text. B's light serif section heads are barely heavier than its body text, so its hierarchy is weaker. A's heading levels are also more distinct. Banding and table structure are essentially equal.

B pairs bold numbered sans headings with a serif body, giving a clear heading/body contrast and comfortable reading. A uses light-weight headings that sit close to the body weight, with rules above each section. A's justified body also forces a hyphenated break in "dash-board". A's rules do add structure, but B's hierarchy reads more decisively.

A pairs bold sans headings with a serif body, so section heads stand out clearly and the body reads comfortably. B uses light-weight headings close in size and weight to its thin body text, which weakens the hierarchy. A's indented body is slightly odd, and its title band sits a little off-centre, but its contrast is stronger overall.

A pairs bold sans headings with a serif body, so the section heads stand out clearly and the text is easy to scan. B uses light serif headings separated by rules. That gives it an elegant look, but the headings are weaker and the body text is small and light, which makes it slightly harder to read. Both have similar bands and spacing.

A keeps every element on one consistent column: the title, rules, Overview, Arabic block and table all share the same margins. B's alignment is erratic. The title is indented, the 'Overview' heading hangs out to the left, and the body text is indented. The second rule and the Arabic heading run off past the right margin, which breaks the edge. B's Arabic text also sits small next to the serif Latin, while A's sans pairing is more even.

B keeps headings and body on one left edge, giving a clean, consistent column. A indents body text far from its headings and adds a rule above every short section, so the page looks fragmented and the left margin feels uneven. A's subordinate References heading does mark it off from the main sections, but B's numbered sections and steady spacing read more cleanly overall.
